# Severity model evaluation

<!-- Generated by Geopolitics.AiEvaluationTests. Do not edit by hand. -->

- Model: `sdca-maximum-entropy/features-1/dataset-1`
- Trained on: 95 labelled cases
- Evaluated on: 45 held-out cases, never trained on
- Comparison baseline: the configured enrichment provider, run over the same held-out cases

> These figures measure how well a small linear model recovers this repository's
> **author-assigned severity rubric** from 95 synthetic examples. That is a real
> supervised-learning result and nothing more. It is not evidence that either system
> can assess the severity of a real geopolitical event, and no figure below should be
> quoted as if it were.

## Head to head

| Measure | Severity model | Enrichment provider |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Accuracy against labels | 0.56 | 0.38 |
| Macro F1 against labels | 0.51 | 0.32 |
| Correct of 45 | 25 | 17 |

The two systems agreed with each other on 18 of 45 cases (40 %).

Agreement is not accuracy: both can agree and both be wrong, which is exactly why
both are scored against the labels rather than against each other. The margin between
the two accuracy figures is the only claim this evaluation makes for the model, and it
is asserted — if the model stops beating the classifier already in the pipeline, the
build fails, because at that point the honest thing to do is remove it.

## Reading these numbers

Synthetic severity fixtures. Every report is invented for this repository and describes no real-world event, vessel, unit, or organisation; place names are real only so the geography is plausible. Labels are author-assigned against the rubric in README.md, not expert-adjudicated. What a model trained on this file learns is that rubric as the author applied it.

Forty-five held-out cases is far too few to quote a confidence interval for. What the
set is good for is detecting a regression: if a change to the features, the trainer, or
the corpus makes these scores drop, something got worse. Treat any single figure here
as a smoke test.

The model is a **second opinion** in the pipeline and never sets the severity an
incident is stored or displayed with. A model trained on a small synthetic corpus has
no business overruling a source that declared its own.
